newsitem.title: ITALY: EU tells Alitalia to sell Malev stake - report.
newsitem.headline: EU tells Alitalia to sell Malev stake - report.

text.p: The European Commission has approved plans by the Italian government to recapitalise troubled flag carrier Alitalia but only on condition the airline sells certain holdings, news agency Ansa reported on Wednesday.
Among these are Alitalia's 35 percent stake in Hungarian national airline Malev.

The Commission ruled last month that a government request to inject some three trillion lire ($1.75 billion) into the loss-making airline should be treated as state aid and therefore subject to strict controls.
It has already decided that the government, which controls Alitalia through state holding IRI, can only inject 2.75 trillion lire into airline coffers.
The state has given the company one trillion lire, with the rest of the cash due to be handed over this year.
Ansa reported that the Commission will only let one trillion be paid to Alitalia now, with a further 500 billion lire due in May 1998 and the remaining 250 billion lire in May 1999.
In addition, Brussels has told Rome it can offer the flag carrier no more funds, or even underwrite loans to the loss-making group.
No one was available at Alitalia or the transport ministry to comment on the report.

Ansa said that as well as the Malev quota Alitalia was being told to sell its remaining five percent stake in aeronautical engineering firm Alfa Romeo Avio, along with holdings in regional airports in Genoa, Naples, Rimini, Florence, Lamezia Terme and Turin.

Alitalia must be given no special treatment when it comes to the allocation of air slots in Italy and the Commission has demanded that an independent coordinator must be appointed this coming winter to oversee Italian slots.
Italy requested Commission permission in 1996 for the Alitalia capital injection and argued that the money should be regarded as a normal market operation and not state aid.

Alitalia bowed to EU pressure earlier this year to cut back its network as part of the recapitalisation plan, reducing its fleet of planes by 14 and cutting some 27,000 flights a year, or 10 percent of operations, off its timetables.
It also promised that it would not offer the lowest price on any route to avoid charges of state-sponsored dumping.

The airline, which chalked up its ninth straight year of losses in 1996, agreed to a rescue package with unions a year ago after months of bitter battle over plans to slash hefty personnel costs and boost productivity.

Commercial director Federico Nucci said last month that Alitalia's current performance was ahead of forecasts. "If we can continue in this actual trend we will not close 1997 at break-even but with a significant profit," he said. $1 = 1,716 lire
